keySentence: Peter Pan never wanted to grow up.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: Peter Pan lived in Neverland where children stayed young forever. He could fly through the night sky and have exciting adventures every day. He fought pirates and played with mermaids and led the lost boys through the forest. Growing up meant leaving all of this behind and becoming serious and responsible. Peter had seen adults and found them dull and forgetful of what truly mattered. He refused to let that happen to himself no matter what anyone else said or thought. Peter Pan never wanted to grow up.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: Peter Pan was the boy who refused to grow up no matter what happened around him. He lived in Neverland, a magical island where adventures happened every single day. He led the lost boys through forests, fought pirates on the open sea, and flew above the clouds. He had no school, no schedules, and no adults telling him what he was supposed to do. When Wendy asked him why he never went home, he said home was for people who had given up on wonder. He had visited the ordinary world once and found it grey and quiet and full of forgotten dreams. Peter chose Neverland not because he was afraid of growing up but because he understood exactly what it cost. Peter Pan never wanted to grow up.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: Among all the characters in children's literature, Peter Pan stands alone in one important way. Most heroes want something they do not have — Peter's defining quality is refusing something he could have. Growing up was available to him, just as it is available to every child who passes through childhood. But Peter looked at adulthood with clear eyes and made a deliberate and fully conscious decision. He had observed adults carefully — their tired faces, their forgotten laughter, their inability to fly. He saw what growing up required a person to leave behind and decided the price was far too high to pay. His choice was not born of ignorance or fear but of a deep and unusual understanding of what life could be. The tragedy and the beauty of Peter Pan is that he was right about what growing up costs and chose anyway. Peter Pan never wanted to grow up.
